assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: FY27 guidance ~18% (budget set in Apr-2026, reiterated 24-Jul-2026, to be reassessed after Q2 on the monsoon); Q1FY27 +15.3% YoY / +3.8% QoQ, Q2 guided at 15-16%. FY26 grew 14.85% against a 15% guide. The MUFG capital lets the company target 18-20% (FY26 annual report). We take 17% in FY27 (as PL and Emkay do) and 18% after, when the new-vehicle, gold and MSME pushes have scale.
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 16.50% FY26; 16.8% annualised in Q1FY27, helped by interest on ~₹38,500 cr of cash and investments parked from the MUFG money. As that liquidity goes into loans and the mix shifts to new vehicles (16-17% of disbursements, targeted at 20-25%) where management is passing on its lower funding cost, we take the yield down ~15-20bp a year.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Fees, commission, fair-value gains and other operating income ÷ average AUM: 0.52% FY26, 0.63% in Q1FY27 (incl. ₹185 cr of gains on liquid funds holding unused MUFG money). Back to ~0.55% as the liquidity is used.
assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense ÷ average of opening and closing borrowings: 8.88% FY26 (company 'cost of liabilities' 8.59% at Mar-26, 8.56% at Jun-26; incremental 7.77% after the Apr-2026 AAA upgrades; bank money ~8%). The underlying FY27E rate is ~8.55%, but the MUFG money cut borrowings in April (₹2,50,690 cr in Mar-26 to ₹2,32,639 cr in Jun-26), so true average FY27 borrowings are ~₹9,000 cr below the engine's opening/closing average; we enter 8.25% so that interest expense matches Q1 actual plus Q2-Q4 at 8.55% on a rising balance (₹20,800 cr). FY28E 8.40% and FY29E 8.25% (≈8.15% / 8.0% on the company basis): new money at 7.8-8.0% replaces older, dearer debt; no rate cuts assumed (repo 5.25%, CPI forecast raised to 5.1%).
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Operating expenses incl. fee and commission expenses and depreciation ÷ average AUM: 2.82% FY26 (2.85% FY25), 2.76% annualised in Q1FY27. ~150 new branches and manpower in FY27 and wage inflation (Q1 staff cost +17%); management expects cost ratios broadly stable as volumes absorb the cost. Small scale gains after FY27. Cost-to-income falls to ~26% because income rises with the extra equity, not because costs fall.
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Impairment ÷ average AUM: 2.22% FY24 (incl. SHFL), 2.18% FY25, 1.89% FY26, 1.90% annualised in Q1FY27. Management guides 'around 2%' on its own basis (credit cost to total assets: 1.65% FY26, 1.66% Q1FY27), so on that yardstick FY26 came in well below guidance. We keep 1.95-2.0% of average AUM (≈1.7% of total assets): the current run-rate plus a margin for a deficient monsoon (IMD forecast 90% of normal, El Nino) and faster growth in MSME and personal loans.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹10.80 a share (₹4.80 interim + ₹6.00 final) = 20.3% of EPS; FY24-FY25 payout 19-23% (FY25 incl. a special from the SHFL sale). The FY26 final dividend was paid on the enlarged share count incl. MUFG's shares (₹1,411.7 cr).
assumptions._minorityPctWhy: No minority interests since Shriram Housing Finance was sold (Dec-2024); subsidiaries left (Shriram Overseas Investments) are wholly owned.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener 'other income' outside operations: ₹52 cr FY26 (₹58 cr before small exceptional items), ₹18 cr in Q1FY27; plus ~₹27 cr pre-tax equivalent of the ~₹20 cr share of profit of the associate Shriram Automall (SFL share FY26 ₹20.5 cr, Q1FY27 ₹5.5 cr), which the engine cannot carry separately.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: MUFG Bank preferential issue: 47,11,21,055 shares at ₹840.93 = ₹39,617.98 cr, allotted 8-Apr-2026 (primary capital; MUFG 20.0% on a fully diluted basis), plus ₹0.89 cr of ESOP exercises in Q1FY27. No further raise is planned: management says the capital supports growth for 4-5 years (Motilal Oswal, 29-Sep-2026) and the FY26 annual report targets a calibrated rise in leverage to ~4.5x over 5-6 years.
assumptions._newSharesWhy: Shares rise from 188.14 cr (FY26 Profit for EPS ÷ EPS; 188.16 cr reported at Mar-26) to 235.29 cr at Jun-26 (Q1FY27 investor update p30): 47.11 cr to MUFG plus 0.02 cr ESOP. EPS uses year-end shares; the allotment on 8-Apr-2026 makes that close to the weighted count.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.15 × 6% = 13.4% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.15: a cyclical lender to small truck operators and MSMEs, above Bajaj Finance's 1.1, tempered by AAA funding and low leverage after the MUFG money). sustainableRoe 16% = the 15-17% the franchise earned in FY24-FY26 (company basis, pre-MUFG) once leverage climbs back toward the company's ~4.5x target over 5-6 years; ROE is only 12.8-13.5% in FY27-FY28 because of the extra equity. g = 10% long-run book growth in the justified P/B. Residual income fades ROE to 16% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.2x FY28E book, ICICI Direct ~2.1x FY28E, Emkay 2.1x FY28E, PL 2.4x Mar-28 adjusted book). 1.5x = own median one-year-forward P/B since Apr-2021 (1.4x, book adjusted for the MUFG issue before it was announced) × the listed-lender move vs five-year medians (−6.6%, Shriram excluded) × the post-merger regime since Apr-2023 (1.6x ÷ 1.4x). Bull 2.0x = close to the Feb-2026 peak (2.1x) and the street; bear 1.2x = where it traded in FY22 before the merger.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (16 − 10) ÷ (13.4 − 10) on book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.4% cost of equity, ROE fading to 16%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only. 9x = median forward P/E since Apr-2021 (9.2x, FY25 EPS taken before the ₹1,489 cr SHFL gain) × listed-lender P/E move vs five-year medians (−17.4%) × post-merger regime (10.8x ÷ 9.2x). Bull = post-merger median 10.8x; bear = 25th percentile since 2021 (7.6x, adjusted).

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: MUFG-backed growth: AUM +19/20/20% (top of the 18-20% ambition), yield +10bp, opex 5bp lower, credit cost ~1.7% of AUM (FY26-type), long-run ROE 18% as leverage rebuilds faster; the market keeps paying close to its Feb-2026 peak.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: A weak monsoon and costlier money: AUM +12/13/13%, yield −30bp (pass-through and competition in new vehicles), funding 30bp dearer (rates rise with inflation), credit cost ~2.6% of AUM (FY25 level plus rural stress); long-run ROE 13%; the multiple falls back to its pre-merger level.

cover.headline: MUFG made Shriram safer and cheaper to fund, not more profitable per share; at the top of its valuation range, the stock already pays for the upgrade
cover.lead: Shriram Finance is India's largest used-truck financier and, since the 2022 merger, a ₹3.1 lakh crore retail lender (47% commercial vehicles, 22% passenger vehicles, 13% small business, the rest two-wheelers, personal, gold and equipment loans) with 3,225 branches and ~1 crore customers. In April 2026 MUFG Bank paid ₹39,618 cr for 20% in new shares, the ratings went to AAA and Q1FY27 profit rose 60%. The street values it on **P/B (2.1-2.4x FY28E book; all Buy, targets ₹1,200-1,250)**. We forecast EPS of ₹61.9 / ₹72.6 / ₹82.6 for FY27-29E but ROE of only ~13-14%, because the new equity takes five to six years to put to work. Applying **1.5x to Sep-28E book of ₹589** (its own 1.4x median forward P/B since 2021, 1.6x since the merger, less the sector's −7% move) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** Every cross-check is also below the price: justified P/B ₹930, residual income ₹825, P/E ₹698. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: MUFG's money lowers risk, not EPS
arguments.p: The ₹39,618 cr issue at ₹840.93 lifted book per share from ₹350 (Mar-26) to ₹449 pro forma and cut leverage from 3.8x to 2.1x. But it is earning only the interest it saves (~8.6% pre-tax): our FY27E EPS of ₹61.9 compares with ~₹63.5 without the deal, and FY27E ROE drops to ~13.2% (time-weighted) from 16-18% before. Management plans to re-lever to ~4.5x only over five to six years.

arguments.h: A real franchise in used trucks
arguments.p: Forty-seven years of lending to small truck owners, valuers in every district, the Shriram Automall auction network and 2,042 rural and semi-urban branches give it an edge in lending against used vehicles that is hard to copy. Loan losses have held at ~1.9% of average AUM through FY26 and Q1FY27. AAA ratings bring new borrowing down to 7.77%, which it uses to win back new-vehicle customers.

arguments.h: But asset quality and margins are not improving
arguments.p: Gross Stage 3 loans are stuck at 4.64% (4.53% a year earlier), high for a large NBFC (Bajaj Finance: 0.96%); MSME (5.2%), construction equipment (7.1%) and gold (2.6%) worsened in the year. Management guides NIM back to ~8.5% over two to three years from 9.04%, as cheaper funding is passed to new-vehicle buyers. A deficient monsoon and the West Asia oil shock are live risks to rural and transporter cash flows.

arguments.h: Priced for a re-rating it has already had
arguments.p: At ₹983 the stock trades at 1.8x our FY28E book and 13.5x FY28E EPS, against medians of 1.4x and 9.2x since 2021. That is close to its Feb-2026 peak while listed lenders have de-rated. The price implies a long-run ROE of ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}}; we forecast 13-14% to FY29E and 16% at best once re-levered. The street's ₹1,218 average target needs 2.1-2.4x book, a multiple the stock has touched only briefly (2.1x forward in Feb-2026).

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management will reassess its ~18% FY27 AUM growth guidance once the monsoon's effect on rural cash flows is known.
Monsoon and kharif output: rainfall was ~12% below normal by late September; a weak rabi season would hit truck utilisation and collections.
Deployment of the last of the surplus liquidity and the first large borrowings at AAA rates (incremental cost 7.77% in Q1; bank money ~8%).
Reappointment of MD & CEO Parag Sharma for five years from 13-Dec-2026 (recommended by the board).
MUFG's 24-month standstill on market purchases runs to around April 2028; any change in its role (more board seats, co-lending, a higher stake) would move the multiple.

sections.title: A truck financier for people banks will not lend to, now with small-business, gold and two-wheeler books attached

blocks.p: Shriram Finance (SFL) lends mainly to the self-employed: small truck owners with one to five vehicles, first-time buyers of a used truck, taxi drivers, small traders and farmers. Most have thin credit records and little paperwork, so banks avoid them. Shriram's edge, built since 1979, is that it can value a ten-year-old truck, knows the borrower's route and customers, and collects in cash if it must. It borrows at ~8.6% (cost of liabilities, Jun-2026), lends at ~16.5-17%, spends ~2.8% of loans on 78,902 staff and 3,225 branches, and loses ~1.9% of loans a year to bad debts. FY26 income was ₹48,133 cr, of which interest ₹46,658 cr.

The business is still mostly wheels: 80.6% of AUM is vehicles or equipment. The Dec-2022 merger with Shriram City Union Finance added MSME loans, two-wheelers, gold and personal loans (now ~25% of AUM). Two-thirds of branches (2,042 of 3,225) are in places with fewer than one lakh people, and they hold 59% of AUM. Two small group companies sit alongside: Shriram Automall India (44.6% owned), which auctions repossessed and used vehicles, and Shriram Overseas Investments (100%), which has an in-principle RBI licence to become a primary dealer in government bonds.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** Shriram earns a high yield because it takes risks others will not: old vehicles, informal incomes, rural cash flows. It has survived every truck cycle since 1979 by pricing that risk and collecting relentlessly, but its loan losses and bad-loan ratios will always be higher than a consumer lender's like Bajaj Finance. The non-vehicle books from the merger diversify it, but they are where asset quality has slipped in the past year (MSME, gold, personal loans).

sections.title: Four decades of truck finance, one transforming merger, one asset sale and a 20% strategic investor

blocks.p: The record shows a lender that grew slowly and safely as a standalone truck financier, then changed shape twice in four years: the 2022 merger that made it a diversified retail lender, and the 2026 MUFG investment that made it a well-capitalised, AAA-rated one. Each change moved the numbers in ways that make simple comparisons misleading, so we list them.

sections.title: Vehicle finance: demand is strong after the GST cut, but the rural economy faces a weak monsoon and an oil shock

blocks.p: Shriram's business follows the truck cycle and the rural economy. Both were healthy going into FY27. Vehicle sales jumped after the GST rate cuts: in Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) commercial-vehicle sales rose 14.1% to 2.65 lakh units (heavy trucks +18.3%, light +20.8%), passenger vehicles +25.9%, two-wheelers +20.3%, tractors +21.6%, and construction equipment returned to growth (+8.8%) after four quarters of decline (Q1 call). Management said truck operators had passed higher fuel costs on to their customers and saw no idle vehicles: "If the utilization levels were a little lower, then sales would not have gone up by 20%".

The risks are macro. The West Asia war pushed up fuel and wholesale prices (WPI 9.87% in June), the RBI cut its FY27 growth forecast to 6.6% and raised its inflation forecast to 5.1%, keeping the repo rate at 5.25%. The IMD cut its monsoon forecast to 90% of normal as El Nino strengthened; rainfall was 24% below normal from 4-Jun to 16-Jul and ~12% below normal by late September. A poor harvest hits Shriram twice: rural borrowers repay less, and truckers carry less freight.

blocks.p: Among listed lenders Shriram is the second largest by market value (₹2.31 lakh crore on 30-Sep-2026) after Bajaj Finance, and the most valuable vehicle financier. Its FY26 returns sit in the middle of the pack: ROE 16.4% (below Bajaj Finance, Cholamandalam and Muthoot, well above M&M Financial and L&T Finance) and ROA 3.3% (above Cholamandalam: higher yields and less debt per rupee of assets). In new vehicles it competes with banks, captive and dealer-linked NBFCs (Cholamandalam, M&M Financial); in used trucks, its home turf, competition is thinner because the work is local and labour-intensive.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** demand is not Shriram's constraint; it grows 15-20% whenever trucks sell. The constraints are the rural economy (a weak monsoon in 2026 is the near-term test), credit discipline in the newer books (MSME, gold, personal loans) and price: as funding gets cheaper, it is choosing to compete for new-vehicle borrowers, where yields are lower.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the biggest change in FY27, the MUFG money, is a balance-sheet tailwind, not an operating one. It makes Shriram safer and lets it grow faster, but each rupee of it earns only the ~8.6% interest it replaces until it is lent out with more debt on top. The operating tailwinds (vehicle demand, cheaper funding) are real but partly competed away; the headwinds (monsoon, mix, sticky Stage 3) are cyclical. That is why we forecast ROE of 13-14%, not a return to 17-18%, through FY29E.

sections.title: Growth: trucks still carry the book; new vehicles, gold and MSME are the add-ons

blocks.p: AUM grew 14.9% in FY26 to ₹3,02,274 cr, in line with the ~15% management said at the start of the year, and 15.3% to ₹3,13,798 cr by Jun-2026. Commercial vehicles supplied over half of FY26's increase. Disbursements were ₹1,84,428 cr in FY26 and ₹49,974 cr in Q1FY27 (+19.5%). The company now has four extra levers: **new vehicles** (16-17% of disbursements from ~10%, targeted at 20-25%, so that new vehicles become 30%+ of the book), **gold loans** (2.4% of AUM, to ~5% in three years from ~2,200 gold-ready branches), **MSME** (13.4% of AUM, to ~20% by expanding beyond the South) and **personal loans** to customers other than two-wheeler borrowers. About 150 branches are to be added in FY27.

The quality of the growth matters more than the rate: the fastest-growing books are new vehicles (lower yield), gold (low loss but small) and MSME (higher yield, higher loss). sections.title: NIM jumps in FY27 because equity replaced debt; management itself expects it to drift back

blocks.p: On our basis (NII ÷ average AUM) the margin was {{fin.nim.10|pct}} in FY25 and {{fin.nim.11|pct}} in FY26; the company's own NIM (on average total assets) was 8.55% and 8.38%. The yield on AUM has held at ~16.5% while the cost of borrowing rose with the FY24-FY25 rate cycle (company cost of liabilities 8.69% in Dec-25, 8.59% in Mar-26). Q1FY27 changed the picture: company NIM jumped to 9.04%, because ₹37,451 cr of MUFG money repaid borrowings in April. Management said ~₹500 cr of Q1's NII came from the new capital, and expects the current NIM to hold for two quarters before easing to ~8.5% over two to three years as new-vehicle loans (lower yield) grow and cheaper funding is passed on.

It does not fade in rupees, but it shrinks as a share of a growing book: by FY29E, with AUM 63% larger and borrowings back up, our NIM is {{F.nim.2|pct}}. Analysts on the Q1 call argued the 8.5% guidance is too conservative; we agree in part (our FY29E NIM is ~9.3% on the company's total-assets basis), but we also take yields down 15-25bp a year because management told us it is using cheaper funding to win new-vehicle customers.

sections.title: Asset quality: bad loans fell from 7% to 4.6% after the merger, and have stopped falling

blocks.p: Gross Stage 3 (non-performing) loans fell from 7.1% in FY22 to 6.2% (FY23), 5.5% (FY24) and 4.55% (FY25), helped by the merger with a cleaner book, write-offs and better collections. Since then the ratio has gone sideways: 4.58% in Mar-26 and 4.64% in Jun-26 (4.53% a year earlier). Net Stage 3 kept improving, to 2.33%, only because provision coverage rose from 43% to 51%. Within the book, commercial and passenger vehicles improved year on year while MSME (4.1% to 5.2%), construction equipment (5.9% to 7.1%), gold (2.1% to 2.6%), personal loans and two-wheelers worsened. Management calls the Q1 rise seasonal and says it sees no stress from fuel prices or vehicle idling.

blocks.p: **A thick provision cushion.** Expected-credit-loss provisions were ₹18,578 cr in Jun-2026, 5.95% of gross loans (5.59% in Mar-25). Even performing (Stage 1) loans carry a 3.45% provision, against ~1.1% at Bajaj Finance, which reflects the higher expected losses of informal, vehicle-backed lending. The cushion means a bad monsoon need not produce a spike in reported credit cost; it does not change the fact that Stage 3 runs at 4.5-5% in a business that lends against old vehicles to informal borrowers.

blocks.callout: **Our forecast:** credit cost of {{F.creditCost.0|n2}}% / {{F.creditCost.1|n2}}% / {{F.creditCost.2|n2}}% of average AUM for FY27-29E against 1.89% in FY26 and 1.90% annualised in Q1FY27. Management guides "around 2%" on its own yardstick (credit cost to total assets: 1.65% FY26, 1.66% Q1), so it has run well inside guidance. Each 10bp of credit cost is ~1.7% of FY28E profit. Bear case: ~2.6% (FY25's 2.18% plus a rural shock).

sections.title: Funding: now AAA, a third from retail deposits, and long on liquidity

blocks.p: Shriram funds itself from five pools. In Jun-2026 borrowings of ₹2,32,640 cr were 31% public deposits (₹72,070 cr from retail savers, a rare licence for an NBFC), 19% bank term loans, 20% foreign borrowings (ECB loans and dollar bonds), 14% securitisation (selling pools of loans to banks) and 14% rupee bonds. The MUFG deal triggered the change that matters most: ICRA and CRISIL upgraded the company from AA+ to AAA on 9-Apr-2026, India Ratings the next day and Fitch to investment grade (BBB-) on 14-Apr-2026. Its cost of liabilities was 8.56% in Jun-2026 but incremental money cost 7.77%, and bank loans should come at ~8%.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** NBFCs fail on funding before they fail on credit, as the 2018-19 squeeze after IL&FS showed. Today it holds three months of repayments in cash (₹17,000-18,000 cr by policy, more in Jun-26), its assets mature ahead of its liabilities, and a third of its money comes from sticky retail deposits. AAA ratings and a Japanese bank as a 20% shareholder add a funding backstop few NBFCs have. Funding is now a strength; the question is only how much of the cost advantage it keeps rather than passes on.

sections.title: MUFG's ₹39,618 cr: good for creditors, fair for shareholders, and a drag on ROE for years

blocks.p: On 19-Dec-2025 the board agreed to sell MUFG Bank 47.11 cr new shares at ₹840.93 each (₹39,618 cr, about USD 4.4 bn) for 20% of the enlarged company. The price was close to the market (weekly close ₹848 on 12-Dec-2025) and 2.4x Mar-26 book; the stock rose ~19% in the next two weeks. Shareholders approved it on 14-Jan-2026 and the shares were allotted on 8-Apr-2026. It is primary capital: every rupee went to the company, which used ₹37,451 cr in Q1 (mostly to repay borrowings) and parked ₹2,167 cr in liquid funds. MUFG has two board seats and, per management, may not buy shares in the market for 24 months; the Shriram group keeps operational control and 20.3%.

Capital adequacy went from 20.4% (Mar-26) to 34.2% (Jun-26) against a 15% minimum, and leverage from 3.8x to 2.1x. The FY26 annual report sets the path: "immediate deleveraging to ~2.6x and a calibrated increase towards an optimal leverage level of ~4.5x over the medium term (5-6 years)". On the same measure (borrowings ÷ equity) our model reaches only {{F.debtEquity.2|n2}}x by FY29E (from {{fin.debtEquity.11|n2}}x in FY26 and {{F.debtEquity.0|n2}}x in FY27E), because 18% growth with a 20% payout lets profit rebuild equity almost as fast as the book grows. Reaching ~4.5x would take AUM growth well above 20% for years, or much higher dividends; management has signalled neither.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the deal was struck at a fair, market price and adds ~24% to FY27E book per share, but EPS is roughly unchanged and ROE falls by ~3.7pp, because the money earns only the interest it saves until it is levered up. sections.title: From ROA to ROE: ~3.5% on AUM levered ~4.5x before MUFG; more ROA but only ~3x leverage after

blocks.p: A lender's return on equity is its return on assets times leverage. Shriram earns a high return on its loans for a vehicle lender (high yields, controlled costs) but has run with modest leverage, so its ROE has been 16-18%, not the 20%+ of the best consumer lenders. The MUFG money raises ROA (less interest to pay) and cuts leverage by more, so ROE falls.

Leverage (average AUM ÷ average equity) falls from ~4.6x to ~3.0x on time-weighted equity, so ROE drops to ~13.2%. From there ROA eases as yields fall, and ROE creeps up only as leverage rebuilds: ~14% by FY29E. Getting back to 16-18% needs leverage back near FY26 levels (~4.6x AUM ÷ equity, 3.8x borrowings ÷ equity); management targets ~4.5x borrowings ÷ equity, but only over five to six years.

sections.title: Profit up 3.7x since the merger year, but ROE has never been above ~18%, and the MUFG money pushes it down to ~13-14%

blocks.p: Before the merger, Shriram Transport Finance (STFC) was a steady, low-growth truck financier: net profit stayed between ₹2,500 cr and ₹2,720 cr from FY18 to FY22, AUM grew 5-9% a year and ROE sank from 20% (FY18) to 11% (FY22) as Covid-era loan losses ran at ~2.8-3.2% of AUM (FY21-FY22). The Dec-2022 merger with Shriram City Union Finance doubled the profit base (₹6,020 cr in FY23) and added small-business, gold, two-wheeler and personal loans. Since then profit has grown ~18% a year to ₹10,024 cr in FY26 (FY25's ₹9,576 cr included a ₹1,489 cr after-tax gain on selling Shriram Housing Finance; before it, FY26 grew ~21%). ROE was 16-18% throughout, good for a vehicle lender but well short of Bajaj Finance or Cholamandalam.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: real in used-vehicle lending and rural reach; not in funding, cost or the newer products

blocks.p: A lender's moat shows up as a lasting gap between what it earns and what it pays for money, staff and bad debts, through a cycle. Shriram has kept ROA at ~3.5% of AUM since the merger with yields of ~16.5% and losses of ~2%, in a segment where many lenders have failed. We test where that comes from and how durable it is.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Shriram has a genuine moat in its core business, lending against used commercial vehicles to small operators: nobody else combines the valuation know-how, the auction network and the rural branch reach at its scale. That moat earns a ~3.5% ROA, not a 5% one, because the model is labour-intensive and the borrowers are risky. The newer businesses from the merger and the push into new vehicles do not carry the same advantage; they add growth at lower returns.

sections.title: Q1FY27: profit +60% on the new capital; guidance held until the monsoon is clear

blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) was flattered by the new equity but solid underneath: AUM +15.3% to ₹3,13,798 cr, disbursements +19.5% to ₹49,974 cr, NII +33.7% to ₹8,056 cr (of which ~₹500 cr from the MUFG money), cost-to-income 25.5% (29.3% a year ago), credit cost 1.66% of total assets (flat), profit +59.8% to ₹3,445 cr and EPS +29% to ₹14.83 (the share count rose 25%). ROE fell to 12.8% on the enlarged equity. Weak spots: Stage 3 up to 4.64%, Stage 2 up in construction equipment, and staff costs +17%. Management kept its ~18% AUM guidance but would "wait for another quarter because the net impact of the deficit in monsoon is a little less known".

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean and well provided, with a few one-offs to strip out

blocks.p: We rate accounting **GREEN**. Joint auditors (M M Nissim & Co and G. D. Apte & Co.) gave unmodified reports; provisions are ~6% of loans; disclosure by product and stage is detailed. Five items deserve attention when reading the numbers:

bullets: **FY25's housing-finance gain.** The sale of Shriram Housing Finance added ₹1,657 cr pre-tax (₹1,489 cr after tax, standalone) in Q3FY25. Reported FY25 EPS was ₹51.92 against ₹44.00 before it; FY26's +2% reported growth was +21% underneath. We use the clean figure in the P/E history.

**Labour Code charge in FY26.** Employee costs include ₹197 cr (₹132 cr gratuity, ₹65 cr leave) from the new definition of wages, most likely booked in Q3FY26 (staff cost ₹1,237 cr that quarter, vs ~₹950 cr in the others). A one-off that depressed FY26 by ~1.5% of profit.

**A change in estimate that flatters opex.** From Jan-2026, dealer commissions on two-wheeler loans are spread over the loan life instead of being expensed upfront: fee and commission expenses were ₹51.5 cr lower in Q4FY26 alone.
**Temporary income on surplus cash.** Q1FY27 included ₹185 cr of gains on liquid funds holding unused MUFG money; it fades as the cash is lent out.

**Screener's FY25 figures do not match the audited accounts.** Its FY25 revenue (₹43,941 cr) appears to include the sold housing business; we replace it with the audited ₹41,834 cr (continuing operations), keeping profit unchanged.

What matters is whether equity keeps up with the loan book. Before MUFG, retained profit grew equity ~13-17% a year (FY24-FY26) against AUM growth of 15-21%, and leverage crept up to ~3.8x. blocks.p: In Jun-2026 the Shriram promoter group held 20.3% (Shriram Capital Pvt Ltd 14.27%, Shriram Value Services 5.68%, Sanlam Life 0.33%, Shriram Ownership Trust 0.01%), unchanged in shares but diluted from 25.38% by the 47.1 cr new shares issued to MUFG Bank, which now owns 20.02% and is classed as a public shareholder. Foreign investors including MUFG held 54.75%, domestic institutions 19.9% and retail 5.03%. Apart from MUFG, the biggest move in the quarter was the Government of Singapore selling 12.7 mn shares (4.47% to 3.04%), while Motilal Oswal MF and New World Fund added. The result is an unusual register: two anchor holders of ~20% each, neither with a majority, and a free float of ~60% that is mostly institutional.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a better company than five years ago, priced as if it were a better business than it is

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's leading used-vehicle financier: ₹3.1 lakh cr of AUM, 3,225 mostly rural branches, ~1 crore customers, 47 years of underwriting used trucks most lenders avoid, losses steady at ~1.9% of AUM, provisions of ~6% of loans, and now AAA ratings, a 34% capital ratio and MUFG Bank as a 20% shareholder. EPS grows ~16% a year to FY29E in our model (profit ~25%, on 25% more shares).

**What you are paying:** 1.8x our FY28E book and 13.5x FY28E EPS, against 1.4x and 9.2x medians since 2021 and 1.6x book since the merger. For that you get ROE of ~13.2-14% to FY29E, because the MUFG equity earns only the interest it saves until it is levered up over five to six years. Our 1.5x Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}), hence SELL; justified P/B (₹930), residual income (₹825) and P/E (₹698) all sit below the price. head: Term
What it means
rows: Non-banking financial company: a lender regulated by the RBI that cannot offer current or savings accounts. A few, like Shriram, may take fixed deposits from the public.
Assets under management: all loans the company manages, including loans sold to banks through securitisation or direct assignment.
Net interest income = interest earned − interest paid. Net interest margin = NII ÷ average AUM (our basis) or ÷ average total assets (company basis, which reads ~0.8-1pp lower).
NII plus fees and other operating income: the lender's "revenue" after funding costs.
Impairment (loan-loss provisions and write-offs) ÷ average AUM (our basis) or ÷ average total assets (company basis).
Ind AS 109 buckets: performing, under-performing (30-90 days overdue) and non-performing (90+ days) loans. ECL = expected credit loss provisions held against them.
Non-performing loans before / after provisions, as % of loans; coverage = Stage 3 provisions ÷ Stage 3 loans.

Total assets (or borrowings, or AUM) ÷ net worth.

assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: FY27 guidance ~18% (budget set in Apr-2026, reiterated 24-Jul-2026, to be reassessed after Q2 on the monsoon); Q1FY27 +15.3% YoY / +3.8% QoQ, Q2 guided at 15-16%. FY26 grew 14.85% against a 15% guide. The MUFG capital lets the company target 18-20% (FY26 annual report). We take 17% in FY27 (as PL and Emkay do) and 18% after, when the new-vehicle, gold and MSME pushes have scale.
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 16.50% FY26; 16.8% annualised in Q1FY27, helped by interest on ~₹38,500 cr of cash and investments parked from the MUFG money. As that liquidity goes into loans and the mix shifts to new vehicles (16-17% of disbursements, targeted at 20-25%) where management is passing on its lower funding cost, we take the yield down ~15-20bp a year.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Fees, commission, fair-value gains and other operating income ÷ average AUM: 0.52% FY26, 0.63% in Q1FY27 (incl. ₹185 cr of gains on liquid funds holding unused MUFG money). Back to ~0.55% as the liquidity is used.
assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense ÷ average of opening and closing borrowings: 8.88% FY26 (company 'cost of liabilities' 8.59% at Mar-26, 8.56% at Jun-26; incremental 7.77% after the Apr-2026 AAA upgrades; bank money ~8%). The underlying FY27E rate is ~8.55%, but the MUFG money cut borrowings in April (₹2,50,690 cr in Mar-26 to ₹2,32,639 cr in Jun-26), so true average FY27 borrowings are ~₹9,000 cr below the engine's opening/closing average; we enter 8.25% so that interest expense matches Q1 actual plus Q2-Q4 at 8.55% on a rising balance (₹20,800 cr). FY28E 8.40% and FY29E 8.25% (≈8.15% / 8.0% on the company basis): new money at 7.8-8.0% replaces older, dearer debt; no rate cuts assumed (repo 5.25%, CPI forecast raised to 5.1%).
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Operating expenses incl. fee and commission expenses and depreciation ÷ average AUM: 2.82% FY26 (2.85% FY25), 2.76% annualised in Q1FY27. ~150 new branches and manpower in FY27 and wage inflation (Q1 staff cost +17%); management expects cost ratios broadly stable as volumes absorb the cost. Small scale gains after FY27. Cost-to-income falls to ~26% because income rises with the extra equity, not because costs fall.
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Impairment ÷ average AUM: 2.22% FY24 (incl. SHFL), 2.18% FY25, 1.89% FY26, 1.90% annualised in Q1FY27. Management guides 'around 2%' on its own basis (credit cost to total assets: 1.65% FY26, 1.66% Q1FY27), so on that yardstick FY26 came in well below guidance. We keep 1.95-2.0% of average AUM (≈1.7% of total assets): the current run-rate plus a margin for a deficient monsoon (IMD forecast 90% of normal, El Nino) and faster growth in MSME and personal loans.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹10.80 a share (₹4.80 interim + ₹6.00 final) = 20.3% of EPS; FY24-FY25 payout 19-23% (FY25 incl. a special from the SHFL sale). The FY26 final dividend was paid on the enlarged share count incl. MUFG's shares (₹1,411.7 cr).
assumptions._minorityPctWhy: No minority interests since Shriram Housing Finance was sold (Dec-2024); subsidiaries left (Shriram Overseas Investments) are wholly owned.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener 'other income' outside operations: ₹52 cr FY26 (₹58 cr before small exceptional items), ₹18 cr in Q1FY27; plus ~₹27 cr pre-tax equivalent of the ~₹20 cr share of profit of the associate Shriram Automall (SFL share FY26 ₹20.5 cr, Q1FY27 ₹5.5 cr), which the engine cannot carry separately.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: MUFG Bank preferential issue: 47,11,21,055 shares at ₹840.93 = ₹39,617.98 cr, allotted 8-Apr-2026 (primary capital; MUFG 20.0% on a fully diluted basis), plus ₹0.89 cr of ESOP exercises in Q1FY27. No further raise is planned: management says the capital supports growth for 4-5 years (Motilal Oswal, 29-Sep-2026) and the FY26 annual report targets a calibrated rise in leverage to ~4.5x over 5-6 years.
assumptions._newSharesWhy: Shares rise from 188.14 cr (FY26 Profit for EPS ÷ EPS; 188.16 cr reported at Mar-26) to 235.29 cr at Jun-26 (Q1FY27 investor update p30): 47.11 cr to MUFG plus 0.02 cr ESOP. EPS uses year-end shares; the allotment on 8-Apr-2026 makes that close to the weighted count.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.15 × 6% = 13.4% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.15: a cyclical lender to small truck operators and MSMEs, above Bajaj Finance's 1.1, tempered by AAA funding and low leverage after the MUFG money). sustainableRoe 16% = the 15-17% the franchise earned in FY24-FY26 (company basis, pre-MUFG) once leverage climbs back toward the company's ~4.5x target over 5-6 years; ROE is only 12.8-13.5% in FY27-FY28 because of the extra equity. g = 10% long-run book growth in the justified P/B. Residual income fades ROE to 16% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.2x FY28E book, ICICI Direct ~2.1x FY28E, Emkay 2.1x FY28E, PL 2.4x Mar-28 adjusted book). 1.5x = own median one-year-forward P/B since Apr-2021 (1.4x, book adjusted for the MUFG issue before it was announced) × the listed-lender move vs five-year medians (−6.6%, Shriram excluded) × the post-merger regime since Apr-2023 (1.6x ÷ 1.4x). Bull 2.0x = close to the Feb-2026 peak (2.1x) and the street; bear 1.2x = where it traded in FY22 before the merger.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (16 − 10) ÷ (13.4 − 10) on book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.4% cost of equity, ROE fading to 16%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only. 9x = median forward P/E since Apr-2021 (9.2x, FY25 EPS taken before the ₹1,489 cr SHFL gain) × listed-lender P/E move vs five-year medians (−17.4%) × post-merger regime (10.8x ÷ 9.2x). Bull = post-merger median 10.8x; bear = 25th percentile since 2021 (7.6x, adjusted).
